samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover every rubric item with concrete structural changes: they slim the banner, collapse the filters, move phone filters into a sticky drawer, cut the grid to 3–4 columns with richer cards, and stay off visual styling. B wins narrowly. It names mobile filter stacking as the likely main cause of the drop, gives a ranked list of quick wins, and adds useful structural ideas such as a list/table view and keeping scroll position on back-navigation. A's list of worst-case scenarios to test is a strong point, but its fixes aren't ranked. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers handle every rubric item well and make close to the same structural recommendations. B is somewhat stronger: it explains why the sidebar and grid scroll out of step, sets a fixed content order for the cards, gives a phone layout that drops quick add and trims the spec line, and lists edge cases to test. A is just as concrete on mobile and pagination, but it gives fewer reasons for the structural problems it names.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover every rubric point well. Each one shrinks the banner and moves the delivery promise into a slim strip, collapses all but 3–5 filter groups, moves to 4 columns with spec lines on the cards, and swaps the stacked phone sidebar for a filter button that opens a sheet. A adds subcategory shortcuts and gives an explicit order for the phone layout. B adds grouping of variant products and keeping the shopper's place when they press back. Neither drifts into visual styling, so the overall quality is essentially equal. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the same core problems and fixes: shrink the banner, collapse the filters, use a filter drawer on phones, go to 4 columns with spec lines on cards, and show 48 per page. B is a bit more concrete. It works out the actual card width (about 150–170px), spells out the phone order, and says what the first screen should hold: breadcrumb, subcategory shortcuts and a toolbar. A has some good extras, such as grouping variants into one card and keeping the shopper's place when they press back, but B's layout guidance is slightly more complete and specific.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make nearly the same diagnosis and offer the same concrete fixes: a mobile filter drawer with a grid-first layout, 3–5 columns with richer spec cards, a 60–80px title row, filter groups collapsed by default, and 36–48 items per page. A is a little tighter and suggests subcategory navigation. B adds a list-view toggle and per-option filter counts. Neither has a clear advantage, and both stay on layout rather than visual style. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same core problems: the mobile filter stack buries the products, six thin cards carry too little information, the banner wastes the first screen and 24 per page is too few. Both give concrete fixes and stay on layout. B is slightly better: it puts the mobile problem first, makes the card problem tangible with the 'Hex bolt M8 £4.20, box of 10 or 200' example, and adds useful structural points such as subcategory navigation, scroll restoration and fixed-height names.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the sidebar and use a phone drill-down. A handles the uneven groups better: team and vehicles become full-width tables that turn into stacked cards on a phone, integrations get their own detail views, and big groups get an 'On this page' list. A also adds useful checks: worst-case content, hiding role-restricted groups and search. B's grouping and URL scheme are good, but it barely covers team members as a large group, and its early '10+ groups' count is inconsistent with its later list of 8. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick the sidebar and give a sound drill-down layout for phones. B goes further on the uneven groups: it treats team and vehicles as tables that turn into cards on a phone, gives integrations detail views, and adds 'On this page' anchors for big groups. B is also more concrete about widths and edge cases. A is clean and buildable but handles only integrations as a special case.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers choose a sidebar with one page per group, give each group its own URL, and describe the same sensible drill-down layout on phones. B ties its reasoning more closely to Driftline's content. It splits pages into narrow form pages and full-width list pages that can grow (vehicles, team, alert rules), and it plans for 200 vehicles, non-admin users and empty states. A treats the pages more uniformly, though its settings search is a useful addition. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the sidebar with one page per group, give each group its own URL and use a drill-down list on phones, so they are close. A does better on the large groups: list-type pages like Vehicles, Team and Alert rules fill the width as tables, while form pages stay in a narrow column, and it flags stress cases such as a company with 200 vehicles. B adds useful extras (a settings search box, an exception for settings that apply instantly, a note on the build) but treats the large groups more lightly.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the sidebar, explain why tabs and one long page lose, and give a drill-down list layout for phones, so they are very close. A edges ahead on rubric item 4: it says the team and vehicles tables can run wider than the form cap, and it limits in-page anchors to long groups. B handles big groups only through card grids and tables. B's search field and merged groups are good ideas, but the rubric doesn't score them. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick the sidebar, use drill-down lists on phones and give similar reasons for rejecting tabs and the long page. B is slightly more buildable: it gives a sticky sidebar and a 40–60ch field cap, explicitly lets the data tables run wider than the forms, and plans for per-integration sub-pages. A has useful touches of its own, such as merging the groups, adding search and showing summary lines on mobile rows. B handles the large groups and the rejected options in a bit more depth.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give four distinct layouts, keep the title and date dominant, compose the banner side by side, and handle the story's safe zones and the poster's viewing distance. A is tighter and more decisive, which suits the request for something short and practical. It also states a clear order for what gets cut as the format shrinks. B hedges on reader names in the story ('if there's room') and runs longer, though its duplication note for the banner and its pre-export checks are useful extras. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give four distinct layouts, keep the title and date dominant everywhere, set the banner side by side and handle the story's safe zones and the poster's viewing distance. B is tighter, which fits the 'short and practical' request. It also gives a clear order for what gets cut as the format shrinks and makes firmer calls, such as dropping the reader list from the story, where A leaves it as 'if there's room'. A's export checklist and its point about the banner repeating the page's own fields are useful, but A is longer than it needs to be.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give distinct layouts, a consistent hierarchy, a correct side-by-side banner, clear drop lists and story safe zones, and both correctly flag that 14 November 2026 is a Saturday. B edges ahead because it keeps type, colour and placement consistent across versions, gives the square post its own layout (title top-left, venue and entry split along the bottom), and adds a practical thumbnail-size readability check. A is equally sound on cropping and safe areas but a little less specific in the square format. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give distinct, practical layouts for all four formats, keep the title and date dominant, and arrange the banner horizontally with mobile-crop advice. B does more on where each format is seen: it gives the poster a 2–3 m reading distance, safe zones for the grid crop and the story, and room for a sticker. B also handles the date better, noting that Friday in November 2026 is the 13th, while A suggests 2025, which has already passed.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give distinct, practical layouts for all four formats, a horizontal banner, a clear list of what gets dropped, and safe-zone guidance. B is stronger because it flags that 14 November 2026 is a Saturday, not a Friday, which is a real error to fix before printing. It also adds useful checks: whether the post reads at thumbnail size, and whether the event page already shows the title above the banner. A is equally thorough on layout and a little more explicit about dropping the address, but it misses the date problem. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers meet the rubric well: each keeps a consistent hierarchy, lays the banner out side by side, says what is dropped in each format, and handles the story safe zones (B also covers poster viewing distance). A wins because it catches that 14 November 2026 is a Saturday, so the stated Friday is wrong for this year, which would prevent a printing error. A's layouts are also slightly more distinct from one another, while B's poster and story are close to the same stack.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a specific ordered sequence, place the proof sensibly and group the features. B is slightly stronger. Each section gets its own kind of visual (invoice mock, oversized tax number, table, type-only quote), and B commits to one big moment instead of leaving the choice open as A does with 'pick one'. B also adds a proof line to the hero and raises sharp practical questions about card fees and tax jurisdiction, while A leans on abstract density labels such as 'woven' and 'open'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give concrete, ordered plans with similar heroes, and both group the features and spread out the proof. A is more decisive: it turns the five features into three beats, makes the large tax number the page's one big moment, and gives each quote a specific place next to the claim it supports. B adds useful mobile and density guidance, but it puts two quotes together and doesn't commit to a single loud section.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a concrete ordered sequence, a specific first screen and quotes spread through the page, so the gap is small. A handles feature weighting slightly better: it groups the features into three chapters and makes receipts the lead. B is ahead on pace: it gives a density label for every section, picks one deliberately 'loud' section, names the breaks it allows, and offers example headlines and the mobile stacking order for the first screen. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both plans are strong and close on most rubric items. A gives every section a pattern and a density state, chooses a single loud section, keeps the alternation explicit, and names its deliberate breaks, so the pacing is more disciplined. B groups the features into chapters well, but it puts the video right after the hero, which delays the problem statement, and its jobs column is a bit lighter than A's density reasoning. A splits the features three-and-two rather than naming one lead feature, which is weaker than B's 'receipts get the biggest treatment'.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a specific, well-reasoned sequence, rank the features instead of giving them equal boxes, and plan deliberate breaks such as a full-bleed video and a loud tax band. A scores better on proof placement: it spreads the three quotes through the page, each tied to the doubt it answers, and gives its tax and pull-quote moments distinct shapes. B is slightly more concrete about the first screen, putting the price beside the button and specifying the mobile order, but it clusters all three quotes next to the comparison, which is close to the proof dump the request warns against. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a concrete, ordered plan with clear section jobs and a well-specified first screen. B spreads the proof better: it assigns each quote a slot (time saved at the top, tax next to the tax estimate, switching near pricing) and gives each section a different shape. A puts the quotes and the comparison next to each other near the end, and admits this weakens the rhythm. A's density mapping and its narrow-screen checks are strong, but B handles proof placement and layout variety better.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep the single-column structure and praise the measure, but Answer A turns a sound layout into more than ten items. It calls two of them launch fixes and adds features the user didn't ask for: breadcrumbs, previous/next links, hiding Subscribe for subscribers, and print/dark mode. Answer B is tighter and more clearly says the layout is mostly fine, with one optional change and a few edge-case checks, though it also goes past three suggestions and proposes captions and previous/next links. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers call the layout sound, keep the single column and say why the measure and type choices work. A proposes one change and frames everything else as edge-case checks, which fits the 'if it's fine just say so' request better. B lists six items and four smaller points, treats two as fixes required before launch, and adds features the user didn't ask about: breadcrumbs, prev/next links, dark mode and print.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers call the structure sound and keep the single column, but both pile on more than three changes and present several as needed before shipping. A opens with a firmer 'ship it', but then lists eight items, including new features the user didn't mention (archive navigation, breadcrumbs, caption slots, prev/next links). B is somewhat tighter and better at explaining why the layout works ('breaks that each have a job'), and it labels its one new feature as optional. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say the single-column structure is sound and both raise the real in-between-width problem for the pull quotes and the wide lead image. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep the single column and avoid a redesign, but both list more changes than the request needed. B says clearly that the layout is sound and ready to ship, and its 'What works' section explains why the measure and the two planned breaks from the column work. A gives only brief praise, has nine items in total, and proposes new features: previous/next archive navigation and caption styles. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A says plainly that the structure is sound and gives reasons for what works, such as the measure, the two deliberate breaks from the column and the reading order. Its six items are more than the rubric's three, and it treats two of them as needed before shipping. B is only 'mostly fine' and gives nine items. It also proposes a new feature (previous/next issue or archive-index navigation) and says less about why the layout works.
